case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: In re Interest of Rylee S.
key_cases.holding: The court held that a dispositional order compelling the mother to release her mental health records and submit to a pretreatment assessment was unreasonable because the juvenile court made no supporting findings of fact and the order did not tend to correct or ameliorate the conditions on which the adjudication was based.
key_cases.relevance: It is the leading Nebraska statement that a court-ordered rehabilitation plan must rest on findings and be reasonably related to reuniting parent and child.
key_cases.quote: we find that the dispositional plan and subsequent order in this case were unreasonable

key_cases.case_name: In re Interest of DeWayne G., Jr.
key_cases.holding: The court held that Neb. Rev. Stat. § 43-283.01 gives a parent no right to demand a separate pre-termination hearing on whether reasonable efforts to preserve and reunify the family were made, and reinstated the termination of parental rights.
key_cases.relevance: It defines how reasonable efforts to reunify are litigated within the ordinary course of the case rather than in a standalone proceeding.
key_cases.quote: the plain language of § 43-283.01 contains no such directive granting a parent or any other party the right to bring a motion requesting a "separate hearing"

key_cases.case_name: In re Interest of Walter W.
key_cases.holding: The court held that the ICWA and Nebraska ICWA 'active efforts' element must be proved by clear and convincing evidence rather than beyond a reasonable doubt, and that the Department met that burden, affirming the termination.
key_cases.relevance: It defines the heightened 'active efforts' remedial and rehabilitative service obligation that replaces ordinary reasonable efforts in ICWA cases.
key_cases.quote: we decline to interpret § 1912(d) — and its Nebraska counterpart, § 43-1505(4) — as requiring the State to prove active efforts beyond a reasonable doubt

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's requirement that States make 'reasonable efforts' to prevent removal and reunify families creates no privately enforceable right under § 1983 or directly under the Act.
key_cases.relevance: Court-ordered service plans cannot be enforced by a private federal action premised on the IV-E reasonable-efforts clause.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

key_cases.case_name: In re Adoption of Micah H.
key_cases.holding: The court held that the Nebraska Indian Child Welfare Act's active-efforts provisions in § 43-1503(1) are not a checklist requiring compliance with every subsection but a case-by-case standard, affirmed the findings of active efforts and of willful abandonment proved by clear and convincing evidence, but vacated the adoption decree because the county court did not strictly comply with the consent and criminal-history requirements of Neb. Rev. Stat. § 43-107.
key_cases.relevance: It defines the content of the active-efforts service obligation as a case-by-case, culturally relevant inquiry judged by the individual circumstances rather than a fixed list of services.
key_cases.quote: The conduct constituting abandonment as defined above must appear by clear and convincing evidence to be willful, intentional, or voluntary, without just cause or excuse.

key_cases.case_name: In re Interest of Becka P. et al.
key_cases.holding: The court held that the orders appointing an educational surrogate were final, appealable orders because they were unlimited in duration and scope and affected the parents' substantial right to direct their child's education, that the juvenile court retained power to issue and rule upon orders to show cause while the adjudications were on appeal, and affirmed.
key_cases.relevance: The juvenile court's appointment of an educational surrogate after the parents refused to sign assessment authorizations shows how far a court-ordered service and evaluation plan can reach into parental decision-making.
key_cases.quote: we conclude these were not temporary orders, but, rather, orders which affected the parents' substantial right to direct the education of their child
